extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institutions' Title IX coordinators, administrators, decision-makers, and advisors (colleges and universities required to comply with Title IX)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements for conducting Title IX grievance processes at postsecondary institutions, including live hearing conduct, cross-examination, admissibility/reliance on statements, decision-maker duties, training, and related recipient obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient-provided advisor when a party lacks one
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party does not have an advisor present at the live hearing, the recipient must provide without fee or charge to that party an advisor of the recipient's choice, who may be, but is not required to be, an attorney, to conduct cross-examination on behalf of that party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provided advisor's role is to conduct cross-examination on behalf of the party; the advisor may but is not required to be an attorney. Recipients may allow advisors to 'represent' parties more broadly, but are not required to do so. This provision ensures that lack of an advisor does not deprive a party of the opportunity to have cross-examination conducted on their behalf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient authority to enforce codes of conduct and replace noncompliant advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the regulations infringes a recipient's ability to enforce its own codes of conduct; if a party's or advisor's conduct (other than Title IX sexual harassment) violates recipient rules, the recipient may respond according to its codes, provided it still complies with §106.45 obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party's chosen advisor refuses to comply with a recipient's rules of decorum (e.g., by yelling), the recipient may provide that party with an advisor to conduct cross-examination. If a provided advisor refuses to comply, the recipient may provide a different advisor. Recipients may adopt rules of decorum applied equally to both parties and may prevent parties/advisors from challenging relevance during the hearing if applied equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-retaliation and confidentiality under §106.71
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.71 prohibits retaliation: no recipient or other person may intimidate, threaten, coerce, or discriminate against any individual for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX or because the individual reported, testified, assisted, or participated in any manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recipient must keep confidential the identity of any individual who has made a report or complaint of sex discrimination (complainants, respondents, witnesses), except as required by FERPA (20 U.S.C. 1232g / 34 CFR part 99), as required by law, or to carry out the purposes of 34 CFR part 106 (including conducting investigations or hearings). §106.71 protects participants against retaliation for exercising rights under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker must explain any exclusion of a question as not relevant during the hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers are required to explain to the party's advisor posing a question any decision to exclude a question as not relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation need not be lengthy or legally technical; a brief statement suffices (e.g., the question calls for prior sexual behavior information without meeting exceptions, or it asks about a detail not probative of any material fact). The explanation increases transparency, helps detect bias, and may reduce appeals. Recipients may adopt rules (applied equally) limiting parties' ability to argue relevance during the hearing or requiring post-hearing revisions to explanations, but the regulation requires an in-hearing explanation. Decision-makers need not be lawyers; training on relevance and rape-shield application is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination must be conducted 'directly, orally, and in real time' at the live hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-examination must occur directly, orally, and in real time during the live hearing; questions may not be required to be submitted or screened prior to the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves live back-and-forth and follow-up questioning unique to cross-examination. Recipients may nonetheless adopt procedures (applied equally) to manage decorum and prevent undue protraction; the decision-maker determines relevance before the question is answered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker must determine relevance before the question is answered and explain exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a party or witness answers a cross-examination or other question, the decision-maker must determine the relevance of the question and explain any decision to exclude it as not relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is combined with the duty to explain exclusions during the hearing and helps ensure only relevant evidence is considered. It is intended to be administrable by trained lay decision-makers using logic and common sense, not to import complex evidentiary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-makers must be trained in issues of relevance and rape-shield protections
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(1)(iii) requires decision-makers (and investigators) to be trained in issues of relevance, including how to apply the rape-shield protections in the regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training is meant to equip often-lay decision-makers to make on-the-spot relevance determinations (including recognizing when questions seek information barred under rape-shield language, privileged information, or treatment records) without importing the complexity of full evidentiary codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-makers must not rely on statements of a party or witness who does not submit to cross-examination (postsecondary live hearings)
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision-maker in a postsecondary live hearing must not rely on statements made by a party or witness who does not submit to cross-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a bright-line rule applying to statements not tested via cross-examination; the Department declined to create exceptions (e.g., statements against interest, family/friend recounting) because applying such exceptions would import complex evidentiary rules inappropriate for lay decision-makers. Where allegations do not turn on party testimony, other evidence (e.g., video) may still be considered. If a complainant files a formal complaint and then refuses to appear or be cross-examined, the complainant's statements (including the formal complaint) are excluded from reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: No adverse inferences may be drawn from a party's absence or refusal to submit to cross-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a decision-maker must not rely on an absent or non-cross-examined party or witness's statements, the decision-maker cannot draw any inferences about the determination regarding responsibility based on such absence or refusal to be cross-examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations were revised to explicitly prohibit drawing inferences from non-appearance or refusal; this helps accommodate Fifth Amendment concerns and fears of retaliation or trauma-driven non-participation. The adjudication may still proceed using other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may hold hearings virtually to facilitate participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have discretion to hold the entire hearing virtually using technology that enables any or all participants to appear remotely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtual hearings can reduce barriers to participation (safety, trauma, geographic constraints) and mitigate some reasons parties or witnesses decline to attend, thereby reducing the incidence of excluded statements due to non-appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of situations where a party does not appear: advisor-only cross-examination and treatment of statements
rubrics_metrics.description: If one party appears and the other does not, a recipient-provided advisor may still cross-examine the appearing party 'on behalf of' the non-appearing party; the appearing party's statements (if tested via cross-examination) may be considered, while the non-appearing party's statements are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party's advisor may appear and conduct cross-examination even when the party themselves does not appear. Because the appearing party's statements were tested via cross-examination, consideration of those statements can yield a fair outcome while respecting the non-reliance rule for absent/non-cross-examined statements. The recipient must provide an advisor for a non-appearing party if the non-appearing party lacks one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude evidence/questions barred by rape-shield, privilege, or treatment-record protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers are under an obligation to exclude questions and evidence barred under rape-shield protections, privileged information, and parties' treatment records; only relevant evidence should be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement to explain exclusions reinforces the duty to apply these protections. The Department emphasized that applying rape-shield and related protections is part of the relevance determination and part of required decision-maker training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply a bright-line non-reliance rule rather than importing comprehensive evidentiary codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because recipients are not courts and decision-makers may be laypersons, the Department prescribes a bright-line rule: do not rely on untested statements, rather than attempting to import complex hearsay and evidentiary exceptions used in courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reasoned that permitting reliance on untested statements (even testimonial vs. non-testimonial distinctions) would undermine cross-examination's truth-seeking function and impose untenable evidentiary complexity on educational institutions. Therefore, untested statements (regardless of whether they would be admissible in court) should not be relied upon in the Title IX grievance process.
